This life-history syndrome renders the species particularly sensitive to anthropogenic pressures, such as habitat fragmentation and poaching.

The ecological role of the Indian pangolin as a specialized myrmecophage is reflected in its morphological and physiological traits. Its strong forelimbs and large claws are adapted for breaching the hard mounds of termites and ants. The nightly foraging activity is energetically expensive, requiring sustained movement across home ranges that can span several hectares. Comparisons with the closely related Chinese pangolin (Manis pentadactyla) indicate that the Indian species attains a heavier body mass, likely reflecting its distribution across the more productive tropical and subtropical zones of the Indian subcontinent. The extended developmental period, including a weaning age of approximately 3 months, allows the juvenile to gradually learn complex foraging techniques from its mother, a crucial skill for survival in habitats where prey availability fluctuates seasonally. Conservation efforts must account for these slow life-history parameters to develop effective recovery plans.
